rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.6 and 3 - a 2-year randomised block field experiment (2018-2019) in a wolfberry orchard on the Tibetan Plateau with three treatments (surface drip alone = CK; flat full-film mulch + surface drip = MF; ridge-furrow full-film mulch + surface drip = MR), measuring soil water content, isotopes, fine roots, yield and WUE. Q2: Section 3.2 / Fig. 3 - soil water contents across the 0-100 cm profile were on average 30.2% (MF) and 37.1% (MR) higher under film mulch plus drip than under drip without mulch over seven sampling occasions; Section 4.2 attributes this to mulching reducing evaporative water loss. Q4: Section 4.4 - the authors report that soil evaporation under MF and MR was lower than under CK (their Table S3), i.e. the intermediate variable (reduced evaporation) through which mulch plus drip raises soil moisture is reported from their own data.
rows.notes: Caveats: (1) the comparator is surface drip without mulch, not a 'traditional irrigation method' as the passage states, so the study isolates the mulch component of DIPM rather than DIPM versus conventional irrigation; a stricter reading could treat this as evidence about mulch only. (2) Of the three effects named in the passage only soil moisture is reported in the main text; soil temperature is referred to only via supplementary Table S3 (not available here) and partly attributed to a cited study (Gu et al. 2016); nutrient availability was not compared across treatments (Table 1 gives site baseline nutrients only). Q3: soil water content measured by one method (gravimetric sampling); isotope-based source partitioning addresses a different variable. Q5/Q6: one site, one soil (sandy loam), one crop, plot scale (1.5 m x 20 m plots). Q7: no stated requirement for the effect; the rainfall-threshold remark is cited from other work. Q8: only 'further study' on nutrients and subsurface irrigation, no limitations of the result stated. Q9: the 30.2%/37.1% soil-moisture differences are reported without SD, CI or range.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.3 and 3.4 - own 2-year field experiment with root sampling by hand auger in 0-100/120 cm layers in October 2018 and 2019 and calculation of fine root length density (FRLD). Q2: Section 3.4 / Fig. 2 - FRLD in the shallow soil layer under drip without mulch (CK) was significantly lower than under film mulch plus drip (MF and MR); overall order of FRLD was MR > MF > CK and root distribution was extended under MF and MR; Section 3.3 / Fig. 5 additionally shows MF and MR trees took a larger share of their xylem water from the shallow layer. Q4: Section 3.2 / Fig. 3 and Section 4.2 - the intermediate variable (shallow soil water content, plus soil temperature in Table S3) was measured and found higher under MF/MR, which the authors link to enhanced root activity in the shallow layer.
rows.notes: Caveats: comparator is drip without mulch rather than a conventional irrigation method, so the study isolates the mulch/ridge-furrow component of DIPM. The study supports only the root-length-density part of the passage (and, via isotopes, greater shallow-water uptake); it reports nothing on crop emergence or growth-period length. Q3: FRLD determined by one method (auger sampling and root measurement). Q5/Q6: single site, soil and crop at plot scale. Q7: the link to soil temperature/root activity is presented as 'possibly' and leans on cited work (Gu et al. 2016; Clarke et al. 2015); no condition stated as a requirement. Q8: no limitations of the root result stated. Q9: Fig. 2 reports Duncan letter groupings; no SD/CI for the treatment difference is given in the text.

notes: Full text available; supplementary Tables S1-S3 and Fig. S1 (referenced for soil temperature, soil evaporation and isotope data) are not included in the provided text. All three treatments use surface drip; the experiment compares film mulch (flat and ridge-furrow) against no mulch under drip, so for both claims the evidence concerns the mulch component of drip-under-plastic-mulch rather than DIPM versus traditional irrigation.
